clue.text: Possibly a lost chance with no small fish

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters may be put in another order
having none of something means that letter is taken away from the group

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be worked on
S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Someone laments a lost chance because the net came up without any small fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the S from A LOST CHANCE, then rearrange the ten letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: The coelacanth is an ancient lobe-finned species once thought extinct, a famous living fossil of the deep sea.

clue.text: Prepare to fire mate

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to raise the hammer of a gun ready for shooting
second meaning: a matey British form of address for a friend

explanation.surface: An order to get a friend ready to shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' looks like the object of 'fire'; it is a separate meaning. In London slang 'me old cock' means my old friend.
explanation.definitionFit: One verb covers readying a firearm's hammer, and the same word is informal British slang addressing a pal.

clue.text: Overhear a chemist admitting pain

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the phrase holds the letters inside itself

parts.note: the run of letters sits across the three words

explanation.surface: An eavesdropper catches a pharmacist confessing to being in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from overh-EAR through A into CHE-mist.
explanation.definitionFit: An ache in the ear is one specific kind of bodily suffering, so the general word covers it.

clue.text: Old? No age limit set presently

indicators.note: to set something is to arrange or put it in order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A question about whether old people are welcome, answered that there is currently no age limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presently' seems to modify 'set' (currently set), but it is the definition in its sense of soon.
explanation.definitionFit: Presently in its older sense means soon or eventually, which the phrase expresses as waiting patiently for the proper moment.

clue.text: Placed statue on empty lorry in a perceptive way

indicators.note: placed means positioned anew, so the letters are put in a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its insides, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: only the first and last letters of lorry remain

explanation.surface: A statue is lifted onto an unloaded lorry, cleverly done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Placed' reads as the verb of the scene but signals rearrangement; in a down clue 'on' puts the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Being astute means shrewd and quick to understand, so acting that way is acting with sharp discernment.

clue.text: Exercises in pitch tail off

indicators.note: one thing sitting inside another means it is placed within it

parts.note: pitch is a black tarry substance
PE is physical education, school exercises

explanation.surface: Training sessions on a sports pitch gradually peter out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' suggests a sports field, but here it is the tar-like substance.
explanation.definitionFit: To taper is to diminish gradually, dwindling toward an end, just as something that tails off fades.

clue.text: Takes off, dismissing odd characters from, say, press

indicators.note: throwing out the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even-placed ones

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A reporter leaves, ignoring the eccentric people in the media scrum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd characters' sounds like strange people, but it means the letters in odd positions of SAYPRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is British idiom for mimicking them, and to ape is likewise to imitate.

clue.text: Condition favouring six to such an extent

parts.note: pro means in favour of
Roman numeral for six
so means to such a degree

explanation.surface: A rule that heavily favours hitting sixes in cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short pieces placed end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: A proviso is a clause in an agreement stipulating a requirement, so it is a condition attached to something.

clue.text: Excalibur perhaps was, and is not going to change

definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally, in Arthurian legend the sword was lodged in a rock
second meaning: the idiom for something fixed and unalterable

explanation.surface: King Arthur's sword story is fixed and will never alter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' flags Excalibur as one example; the legend has Arthur draw the sword from a stone, though some versions differ.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a decision or rule that is fixed permanently, like carved lettering, so it will not alter.

clue.text: Simple band from London line left at the end

parts.note: the Circle line is a London Underground line

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A plain ribbon was left behind on a London Tube line at the terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the abbreviation L, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A circlet is a plain ring or headband, typically worn round the head as an ornament, so an unadorned band.

clue.text: Faint moody expression about a case of shingles

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: a pout is a sulky facial expression
taken as written

indicators.note: a case is the outside covering, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A patient with shingles looks weak and sulky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faint' could be an adjective, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To faint is to lose consciousness briefly, and the phrasal verb is the everyday way of saying someone collapsed unconscious.

clue.text: Substitute goalie's first class arrangement with bank

parts.note: a stand-in is a replacement

indicators.note: the first of something is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
an order is a class or rank, as in biology or society

explanation.surface: A reserve goalkeeper gets a top-rate deal with a bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First class' reads as one phrase meaning excellent, but 'first' belongs with the goalie and 'class' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A standing order is an instruction to a bank to pay a fixed sum regularly, a British term for a recurring payment.

clue.text: Dismay of company people having to accept authoritarian

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a nation is a people
stern means strict and severe

explanation.surface: Staff are dismayed at having to accept a dictatorial boss.
explanation.walkthrough: CO comes first; the bossy word then goes inside the word for a people, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Consternation is anxious alarm and shock, which is what dismay describes as a sudden distressed feeling.

clue.text: Rock group gets none and he must be upset!

indicators.note: upsetting something knocks it over and disorders it, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A band's frontman is upset that it receives no royalties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock group' looks like a band, but it is a literal group of rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Stonehenge is the prehistoric circle of standing stones in Wiltshire, England, literally an arrangement of massive stones.

clue.text: Plants whistle-blower to infiltrate works

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside, so one piece enters another

parts.note: toils means works hard
a referee blows the whistle

explanation.surface: A company plants an informant to infiltrate a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plants' looks like a verb and 'whistle-blower' an informant; the first is the definition and the second a referee.
explanation.definitionFit: Trefoils are clover-like herbs with three-part leaves, so they are examples of the wider group of flora.

clue.text: Clever answer right for the French

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
droit is the French word for right

explanation.surface: A quick-witted reply that suits French speakers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the French' asks for the French translation of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Adroit means skilful and quick-thinking, a close synonym of smart or clever in handling things.

clue.text: Takes in top paper

parts.note: to take someone in is to deceive them
a cap is a top or lid

explanation.surface: Someone accepts the best newspaper, or brings in the top sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes in' looks like a container signal, but it is a verb meaning deceives.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolscap is a large traditional size of writing sheet, once watermarked with a jester's hat, so a kind of stationery.

clue.text: Numbers must be inclusive of irate people always on the move

indicators.note: including something means holding it within, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: Nos is the abbreviation for numbers
mad means angry

explanation.surface: A diversity policy says staff counts must include angry people who keep moving about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' could be digits, but its abbreviation is the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomads are wandering peoples with no fixed home who travel from place to place, never settling.

clue.text: Artist diplomat is serious about?

indicators.note: the letters are to be found about, that is spread around within, the words given

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an envoy is really in earnest about something.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from diplo-MAT through IS into SE-rious.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was a leading French painter of the twentieth century, so an example of the category.

clue.text: Shenanigans — performing after international gets into medals

indicators.note: coming after means being placed later in the sequence
getting into something means entering it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: gongs is British slang for medals or honours
I is the abbreviation for international
a performer on stage is on

explanation.surface: An international athlete's antics after playing in the medal events.
explanation.walkthrough: The medals word holds the international letter, and the performing word follows the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Goings-on are suspicious or improper activities, the same as mischievous shenanigans.

clue.text: Confess — keeping family, and going down

indicators.note: keeping something means holding on to it, so one piece holds another

parts.note: to sing is slang for confessing to the police
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: A criminal admits everything to protect relatives, and faces going down to prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going down' suggests a prison term, but here it is the definition in its literal sense of descending.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinking describes descending, especially through water, which matches moving downward.

clue.text: Inflation should hold this up

parts.note: surface reading: rising prices ought to delay some economic event
setter's reading: filling a craft with warm gas keeps it aloft

explanation.walkthrough: 'Inflation' reads as economics and 'hold up' as delay; both are literal, filling with gas and keeping aloft.
explanation.definitionFit: This aircraft is an envelope filled with heated gas, and staying inflated keeps it suspended in the sky.

clue.text: One may be dropped in race for staff

definitions.text: One may be dropped in race
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the stick passed between runners in a relay
second meaning: a stick or rod, such as a truncheon or conductor's wand

explanation.surface: Someone might be dropped from a race to make way for other personnel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' seems to mean employees, but it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A baton is a short rod carried by relay runners, conductors or police, so it is a kind of stick.

clue.text: Understanding about European lament

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: ken means knowledge or understanding
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Sympathy for a European's sorrowful song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' is usually eager; here it is a noun, an Irish wailing for the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A keen is a traditional Irish funeral wail, a mournful cry of grief for someone who has died.

clue.text: Name a second coin that's emerging

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for name
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for second
a cent is a small coin

explanation.surface: A collector is asked to identify a second new coin now coming into circulation.
explanation.walkthrough: Four short pieces placed in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Nascent means just coming into existence and beginning to develop, as something newly appearing is.

clue.text: Set of laws protecting a German painkiller

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a code is a body of laws
ein is German for a

explanation.surface: Legislation shields a German man who sells drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A German' is not a person but the German word for 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Codeine is an opium-derived analgesic drug used to relieve moderate aches, so it is a medicine for pain.

clue.text: Costs incurred and claimed by people once married?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: informal short form of expenses

explanation.surface: Divorced spouses run up and demand money for bills.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence about alimony, but it splits into two meanings. Exes is British slang for work expenses.
explanation.definitionFit: The same plural is informal British shorthand for reimbursable spending, and also means former husbands or wives.

clue.text: Get boring after picture, seeing this in bed

indicators.note: coming after means being placed later in the order

parts.note: a snap is a photograph
to drag on is to become tediously long

explanation.surface: Watching a film in bed becomes tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' suggests sleeping, but it is a flower bed; the definition is cryptic.
explanation.definitionFit: The antirrhinum is a common garden flower grown in borders, so one would spot it in a planted plot.
